notes.meaning: God commands Moses to make two gold rings for the top corners of the breastpiece. Two braided gold chains were then looped through these rings and anchored to the gold settings on the shoulder straps of the ephod. This kept the top part of the sacred chest piece hanging firmly from Aaron's shoulders as he served.

Two more gold rings were attached to the inside lower corners of the breastpiece, and a matching pair was sewn onto the front of the ephod just above the waistband. A blue cord laced these lower rings together so the chest piece stayed firmly in place against the ephod without shifting or swinging outward. This showed that the high priest's holy garment of service and his role of carrying the people before God were bound tightly together.

Whenever Aaron entered the Holy Place, he carried the names of the twelve tribes over his chest on the breastpiece. This reminded everyone that the high priest never came before God in his own name, but as the representative of all the people. In Scripture, carrying someone on your heart means loving them deeply and caring for their needs.

The Urim and Thummim, meaning lights and perfections, were placed inside the folded breastpiece over Aaron's heart. Through these sacred objects, God gave clear guidance and answers when the nation faced difficult choices. They reminded Israel that the Lord was their true King, giving wisdom to lead His people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition views the Urim and Thummim as a sacred lot kept in the breastpiece pouch to reveal God's will, which ceased after the Babylonian exile.

notes.meaning: Aaron wore an all-blue robe directly beneath the ephod, woven in one solid piece with a center opening for his head. The neck opening was reinforced with a strongly woven collar like a coat of armor so it would not tear when put on. The heavenly blue color pointed to the pure and heavenly character of the priest's sacred calling.

The hem of the blue robe was trimmed with crafted pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, alternating with bells of pure gold. As Aaron walked and ministered, the bells jingled softly between the colorful fruits. These ornaments pictured the beauty, fruitfulness, and joyful message of serving the Lord.

Aaron was required to wear this bell-trimmed robe whenever he ministered so its sound was heard as he entered and left the Holy Place. Hearing the bells let the worshipping crowd outside follow his movements in prayer, and following God's commands kept the priest from death. It taught that people must approach the holy God with deep reverence and obedience.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular tradition claims that a rope was tied to the high priest's ankle so his body could be pulled out if the bells stopped ringing inside the sanctuary.

notes.meaning: Moses was instructed to make a plate of pure gold and engrave it like an official seal with the words HOLY TO THE LORD. This shining plate was tied with a blue cord to the front of Aaron's linen turban so it rested across his forehead. It openly proclaimed that the high priest was set apart entirely for God's honor.

The gold plate remained on Aaron's forehead so that he could take away the guilt that touched even the holy gifts brought by the people. Because human offerings are never completely flawless, the consecrated priest stood as a go-between so that God would gladly accept their gifts. This pointed to Christ, who pardons the imperfections in our worship and makes us pleasing to God.

The high priest's inner tunic and turban were woven out of fine white linen, held together by an embroidered sash. The long tunic covered his whole body down to his feet, and the sash wrapped around his waist for active duty. The clean white linen stood for the purity and righteousness required in God's presence.

Aaron's sons were also given white linen tunics, sashes, and special headbands made for honor and beauty. While their clothes were simpler than the high priest's ornate vestments, they clearly marked them as official servants of the Lord. Their clean garments showed the dignity of serving in God's courts.

Moses was told to clothe Aaron and his sons in these garments, anoint them with oil, and officially consecrate them for their work. The phrase used for ordaining them means to fill their hands, picturing them receiving their holy duties and offerings to present to God. This public ceremony set them apart from the rest of the community to serve the Lord as priests.

The priests were commanded to wear linen undergarments reaching from the waist to the thigh to cover their bare skin. They had to wear them whenever they came near the altar or entered the Tent of Meeting, or they would incur guilt and die. This lasting rule ensured modesty in God's house, standing in sharp contrast to the immodesty of pagan worship.
